On the global scale, these boundaries are often geopolitical and grounded in economic landscapes; at the state level, the focus may revolve around ongoing nation-building and national identity; and at the local scale, boundaries are both tangible and perceived, falling within the realm of everyday life experiences. Building upon this categorization, we focus on how different boundaries in the Arctic operate across different scales and become increasingly porous due to ongoing environmental changes, which puts their relevance into question.

For example, Arctic cooperation and knowledge regarding the bio-accumulation of persistent organic pollutants (Rottem, Citation2017) or the Agreement on the Conservation of Polar Bears (1973) showcase policies driven rather directly and efficiently from scientific endeavors (Brower et al., Citation2002). On the other hand, policy-based science is motivated or prioritized based on other goals by policy agendas or the need to address specific policy areas. This could lead to selective knowledge in order to fit pre-existing beliefs or influence power relations. For instance, the prioritization of oil and gas exploration in the Arctic (Gautier et al., Citation2009), driven by considerations of energy security, geopolitics, and economic interests, exemplifies how policy objectives intertwine political and environmental realms in the region. 3. The many Arctics of the Anthropocene

In this section, we examine the demarcation process that resulted in the first internationally-shared operational definition of the Arctic. We then explore how ongoing changes in both the natural and human environments are challenging the suitability of this definition (Stephenson, Citation2018).

. However, in contrast to the Antarctic which is defined fairly directly based on the land surrounding the South Pole (Nowlan, Citation2001), no omnipotent definition of the Arctic or even its involved states exists, and rightly so. Conceptually, the Arctic refers to multiple constellations and scales (e.g. high Arctic, low Arctic, sub-Arctic; Hamelin, Citation1968), ranging from natural, objective, and calculable definitions (e.g. phytogeographic boundaries such as the tree line or the presence of permafrost, climatic boundaries based on average temperatures or the extent of sea ice; Linell & Tedrow, Citation1981; Stonehouse, Citation1989; Woo & Gregor, Citation1992), to places and latitudes (e.g. north of the Arctic Circle at about 66°33′N; O'Rourke, Citation2011), to imaginaries and socially constructed ideas of Arctic environments and cultures (Lehtinen, Citation2019; Saarinen & Varnajot, Citation2019; Tennberg, Citation2022). It is only after World War II, with the threat of the cold war and the generation of systemic knowledge about the Arctic's role in the climate system, that the Arctic became the global indicator of contemporary change (Sörlin, Citation2017).
